answer_text:
Let \(\mathcal{F}_n=\sigma(X_0,X_1,\dots,X_n)\). Since the \(X_n\) have finite means, \(S_n=\alpha X_n+X_{n-1}\) is integrable.

For \(n\ge 1\),

\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb{E}[S_{n+1}\mid \mathcal{F}_n]
&=\mathbb{E}[\alpha X_{n+1}+X_n\mid \mathcal{F}_n] \\
&=\alpha\,\mathbb{E}[X_{n+1}\mid \mathcal{F}_n]+X_n \\
&=\alpha(aX_n+bX_{n-1})+X_n \\
&=(\alpha a+1)X_n+\alpha bX_{n-1}.
\end{aligned}
\]

For \(S_n\) to be a martingale, we need

\[
(\alpha a+1)X_n+\alpha bX_{n-1}=\alpha X_n+X_{n-1}.
\]

Rearranging,

\[
(1-\alpha b)(X_n-X_{n-1})=0.
\]

Thus, in general, we require

\[
1-\alpha b=0,
\]

so

\[
\alpha b=1.
\]

Since \(a+b=1\), this gives the required value

\[
\boxed{\alpha=\frac{1}{b}}
\]

provided \(b\neq 0\). If \(b=0\), no finite such \(\alpha\) exists in general.
